The S chart limits are UCL = B4 × S̄ and LCL = B3 × S̄ , and the mean chart uses A3 × S̄ . (The 2010 copy of the sheet misprinted B4 for both; version 1.4.2 has it right.)
Plots cumulative deviations from a target
Plots the cumulative sum of deviations from a target. Each new point adds to the running total, so small consistent departures pile up and become visible.
Detects small, sustained shifts faster than Shewhart charts; slower for large shifts
Detects small, sustained shifts faster than a Shewhart chart (Xbar, individuals). It is slower for large, sudden shifts.
Typical starting parameters: target, reference value k (about 0.5σ), decision interval h (about 4 to 5σ). These are design choices, not fixed thresholds.
Typical starting values: a target , a reference value k (about 0.5σ ), and a decision interval h (about 4 to 5σ ). These are design choices, not fixed thresholds.
"Detect a small persistent drift": CuSum or EWMA.
When a question says "detect a small persistent drift," the answer is CuSum or EWMA.
The CuSum on the reference sheet
CuSum on the reference sheet (standardized): Sₙ = (1 ÷ σx) × Σ(xᵢ − T), the running sum of deviations from target T, in σ units

The sheet gives a standardized version: Sₙ = (1 ÷ σx) × Σ(xᵢ − T) , where T is the target and σx the process standard deviation. It is the running total of deviations from target, measured in σ units. Example: target 50, σ = 2, readings 52, 51, 53. Deviations 2, 1, 3, total 6. S = 6 ÷ 2 = 3.0.
EWMA on the reference sheet: EWMAₜ = λ·Yₜ + (1 − λ)·EWMAₜ₋₁, with λ greater than 0 and at most 1, and EWMA₀ = target or historical mean

EWMAₜ = λ × Yₜ + (1 − λ) × EWMAₜ₋₁ (this is on the reference sheet), where λ is greater than 0 and at most 1, and EWMA₀ is the target or the historical mean. Each point is a weighted average of the newest reading and all earlier ones, with recent data weighted most.
λ typically 0.05 to 0.25 (a common choice, not fixed); control limits about 3σ of the EWMA statistic
λ is typically 0.05 to 0.25 (a common choice, not fixed). Small λ gives more smoothing and better detection of small shifts. Control limits are about 3σ of the EWMA statistic.
Detects small shifts; weights recent data more heavily; fairly robust to non-normality
Detects small shifts , weights recent data more heavily, and is fairly robust to non-normality.
CuSum vs EWMA vs Shewhart: small shifts favor CuSum/EWMA.
For small shifts , favor CuSum or EWMA. For large, sudden shifts, a regular Shewhart chart is fine.
Western Electric rules: 1 point beyond 3σ; 2 of 3 beyond 2σ (same side); 4 of 5 beyond 1σ (same side); 8 in a row on one side of center
A signal is: One point beyond 3σ. Two of three points beyond 2σ (same side). Four of five points beyond 1σ (same side). Eight in a row on one side of the center line.
Nelson tests (Minitab): 1 point >3σ; 9 in a row on one side; 6 trending; 14 alternating; 2 of 3 >2σ; 4 of 5 >1σ; 15 within 1σ (stratification); 8 beyond 1σ both sides (mixture)

One point beyond 3σ. Nine in a row on one side of the center line. Six in a row steadily increasing or decreasing (a trend). Fourteen in a row alternating up and down. Two of three points beyond 2σ (same side). Four of five points beyond 1σ (same side). Fifteen in a row within 1σ of the center line (either side), which suggests stratification or limits that are too wide. Eight in a row beyond 1σ on either side, which suggests a mixture of two populations.
Common cause means leave alone and improve the system. Special cause means investigate and react.
Common cause: natural variation. Leave it alone and improve the system if the level is not acceptable. Special cause: an assignable event. Investigate and react.
Control limits are not spec limits
Control limits are not spec limits. 3σ limits give about a 0.27% false-alarm rate per independent point; using several sensitizing rules together raises the overall false-alarm rate.

Control limits come from the process. Spec limits come from the customer. A 3σ limit gives about a 0.27% false-alarm rate per independent point. Using several sensitizing rules together raises the overall false-alarm rate.
Chart selection by data type (see SG-0)
By data type and subgroup size (see the selection tree at the top of this file).
Other control methods: standard work, training, documented procedures, audits, process-owner handoff
Charts are one method. Others include standard work, training, documented procedures, audits, and handoff to the process owner.
Read the chart and choose the action
Given a chart, identify the rule violated and decide the correct action (investigate vs leave alone).
Given a chart, name the rule that was violated and decide: investigate (special cause) or leave alone (common cause).

Anatomy: plotted statistic, center line, UCL/LCL at ±3σ of the plotted statistic, and zones A (2 to 3σ), B (1 to 2σ), C (center to 1σ) used by the sensitizing rules. σ of the data differs from σ of the statistic (σ/√n for subgroup means).

A chart has the plotted statistic , a center line , and UCL and LCL at ±3σ of the plotted statistic. The space between is divided into zones : Zone A (2 to 3σ), Zone B (1 to 2σ), and Zone C (center to 1σ). The sensitizing rules use these zones. Note that the σ of the data differs from the σ of the statistic : for subgroup means, the plotted statistic has σ ÷ √n.
Western Electric (8 in a row on one side) and Nelson/Minitab (9) are different rule systems, not contradictions. Use one set per question and do not mix them.
Western Electric (8 in a row) and Nelson or Minitab (9 in a row) are different rule systems, not contradictory. Use one set per question and do not mix them.
Minitab applies only the beyond-limits test on time-weighted charts (EWMA, CuSum)
Minitab applies only the beyond-the-limits test on time-weighted charts (EWMA and CuSum).
Do not recompute limits just because a point is out
Do not recompute limits because a point is out of control. Investigate the assignable cause; recompute only after a verified process change and a stable baseline.
Investigate the assignable cause. Recompute limits only after a verified process change and a stable baseline. Deleting points and re-limiting to make a chart look in control hides the problem.
Inside the limits is not the same as in control
A point inside the 3σ limits can still violate a run or trend rule; 'all points within limits' does not prove control
A point inside the 3σ limits can still violate a run or trend rule. "All points within limits" does not prove control.
Cost of controls versus the benefit
Compare the cost of sustaining controls (monitoring, training, audits) to the benefit of preventing regression

Controls are not free. Compare the cost of sustaining them (monitoring, training, audits, inspection, software) with the benefit of preventing the process from sliding back. A control that costs more than the loss it prevents is not worth keeping.
ROI and payback logic carried from 1.3.3
Use the same tools as in SG-1.3. ROI = (benefit − cost) ÷ cost. Payback = investment ÷ annual benefit (assuming a steady yearly benefit).
Include both hard and soft benefits, and ongoing costs
Count both hard and soft benefits , and include ongoing costs , not just the upfront cost. A control with a small purchase price and a large yearly labor cost can be more expensive than it looks.
Is a costly control justified? Compare expected savings with the cost of control.
Compare the expected savings the control protects with the total cost of the control. The expected loss without the control is the savings at risk times the chance they slip away.
Process step, characteristic (CTQ), specification/target, measurement system, sample size and frequency, control method, owner, reaction plan, document reference

For each key process step, a control plan lists: the process step the characteristic (CTQ) being controlled the specification or target the measurement system (and that it has been validated) the sample size and frequency the control method (a control chart, a poka-yoke, an SOP) the owner (who is responsible) the reaction plan (what to do when something goes wrong) a document reference (where the procedure lives)
Supporting items: SOPs, training, process owner, transition plan
SOPs , training , a named process owner , and a transition plan for the handoff from the project team.
A living document owned by the process owner
The control plan is owned by the process owner and updated as the process changes. It is not filed away at project close.
A control plan is missing a reaction plan or an owner. Identify what is wrong.
Check the list above. The most common gaps are a missing reaction plan and a missing owner.
Trigger (out-of-control signal or rule), immediate containment, who acts, investigation, corrective action, escalation, documentation, resume

A response plan covers: the trigger (an out-of-control signal or a rule violation) immediate containment (stop bad product moving on) who acts investigation to find the cause corrective action escalation if it cannot be resolved quickly documentation resuming normal operation
Decision rules for out-of-spec product disposition
The plan states the rules for handling nonconforming product: segregate it , then decide to sort, rework, scrap, or accept as is , with named authority for each decision.
Which action follows an out-of-control signal? Contain, investigate, correct, document.
Contain, investigate, correct, document. Containing comes first so that suspect product does not reach the customer.
Out of control is not out of spec

Out of control is not out of spec: a point can signal a special cause while within spec, and a stable process can still produce out-of-spec output. Response plans differ: investigate a special cause vs redesign the process.

A point can signal a special cause while still within the spec. Investigate the cause even though the part would pass. A stable process can still produce out-of-spec output if its natural variation is too wide or off target. The responses differ: investigate a special cause , versus redesign or improve the process itself.
